analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas drilling leases off California's coast.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 with 37 Democratic cosponsors, the California Clean Coast Act has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee with no hearing, no vote, and no action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently prohibit new oil and gas leasing, preleasing, and related activities in federal waters off California's coast, locking the ban into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. It would not touch rights under leases already issued, so drilling under existing leases could continue. Introduced by Rep. Salud Carbajal with 37 Democratic cosponsors, it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: California's coastal communities, beachgoers, and the tourism and fishing businesses that depend on an unpolluted coastline would gain lasting protection from new offshore drilling and the spill risk that comes with it. State and local governments that would bear cleanup and economic costs after a spill would also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: California coastal communities, tourism and fishing businesses

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits new oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in federal waters off California's coast, a stronger and more durable protection than the temporary bans Congress has passed in the past.
Because the ban is written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself, it cannot be undone by a future administration's leasing plans the way a presidential withdrawal can.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to new federal leases off California, and the federal government forgoes the bonus bids and royalties new leases would have generated. Existing leaseholders lose the prospect of expansion into new acreage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil and gas companies; federal lease revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill does not affect rights under leases issued before its enactment, so existing oil and gas operations off California would continue, and the spill risk from those operations would remain.

A permanent ban closes off federal waters off California to any future energy production and to the federal revenue that leasing there would generate, which critics see as unnecessarily foreclosing options for domestic energy supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but narrower than the bill's name suggests: it prevents new drilling off California without addressing the roughly two dozen existing leases already allowed to operate. The cost — forgone leasing revenue and foregone potential production from one state's federal waters — is modest for the country but meaningful to the offshore oil industry. For the coastal communities the bill protects, the trade favors the ban.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, joined by 22 original cosponsors, nearly all California House members, including Aguilar, Huffman, Garamendi, Levin, Lofgren, and Swalwell.
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, April 10, 2025.
A total of 37 House Democrats have signed on as cosponsors, all of them California members of Congress.
Since that referral, the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has won or lost: current law is unchanged, and oil and gas companies retain whatever possibility exists under existing law for future leasing off California, while coastal communities remain without the permanent protection the bill would give them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one — current law stands unchanged

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban new oil and gas leasing off California's coast.

for.name: 37 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Rep. Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which has sat in committee since its April 2025 referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 37 cosponsors are Democrats — every one a California member — and no Republican has signed on; no votes have occurred, but the bill sits with a Republican-chaired committee and a Republican House majority.

industries.note: The bill permanently bars the industry from obtaining new federal leases off California, though existing leases remain valid and producing. What the industry could gain from expanded drilling — and the spill risk coastal communities would bear — run directly against each other.

industries.industry: California coastal tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: Blocking new drilling protects beaches, fisheries, and the tourism economy from the disruption and spill risk that new offshore platforms would bring. Their interest runs alongside that of coastal residents.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no committee action in the months since referral, and with Republicans holding a 223-seat House majority and chairing the Natural Resources Committee, a hearing or floor vote is unlikely. Unless it advances unusually, it will die when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, and its backers would need to reintroduce it in the next Congress.
